title: Path Params, Query Params, Headers, and Bodies
summary: Read every part of a request, from path and query parameters to headers and JSON bodies, and shape the JSON you send back.
intro: A route gets a request to the right handler. Then the handler has to read it: which room, which filters, which page, who's asking, and what they sent. That information arrives in five places, each with its own rules, and almost everything a client sends arrives as plain text that has to become real Java values. Read it carelessly, and you get the classic API bugs: lists that skip items, a body that's silently refused, an update that wipes a field. This lesson goes through each place in turn, the path, the query string, the headers, and the body, then ends with the other half of the job: the JSON Roombook sends back.

steps.title: Where request data lives
steps.body:
Every piece of information in a request has a place where it belongs, and putting it in the right one isn't just tidiness. Caches, logs, browsers, and proxies all treat each place differently, so the place decides who sees the data, what gets saved, and what can be bookmarked or shared.

```diagram request-data-parts
Each place has one job. Everything but the body arrives as plain text.
```

## Five places, five jobs

- **The path** says which thing: `/v1/rooms/3` is room 3. It's the resource's identity, so it's what gets bookmarked, linked, and cached.
- **The query string**, the part after `?`, holds options for reading: which rooms to include, in what order, which page. `/v1/rooms?building=main-library` is still the list of rooms, seen through a filter.
- **Headers** describe the request itself: what format the body is in, what format the client wants back, who's calling, and conditions like only if it changed.
- **The body** carries the content of a POST, PUT, or PATCH: the booking to make, the fields to change.
- **Cookies** carry the session, recall from the web course: the browser sends them back in a `Cookie` header on every request to the site. The lesson on logins builds Roombook's sessions on them.

One rule follows from this: never put secrets in the URL. Paths and query strings end up in server logs, in browser history, and in the logs of every proxy along the way. Passwords, tokens, and keys go in headers, which those tools don't save by default.

## How Spring hands each one to you

Spring MVC gives a handler each part through an annotated parameter:

| Place | In Spring | For `/v1/rooms/3?limit=20` |
|---|---|---|
| Path parameters | `@PathVariable` | `String roomId` is `"3"` |
| Query string | `@RequestParam` | `int limit` is `20` |
| Headers | `@RequestHeader` | `@RequestHeader("Accept") String accept` |
| Body | `@RequestBody` | a record, read from JSON by Jackson |
| Cookies | `@CookieValue` | `@CookieValue("__Host-session") String session` |

A parameter can also take everything at once: `@RequestParam MultiValueMap<String, String>` gets the whole query string, and `@RequestHeader HttpHeaders` gets every header.

## It's all text

The path, the query string, and the headers are plain text, every character of them. When you declare a parameter as `int` or `long`, Spring converts the text for you, which is handy, and it's also where the surprises are: text that isn't a number gets a 400 from Spring before your handler runs. The routes lesson showed it for a path, and the next part shows it for a query.

The JSON body is different. JSON has its own types, numbers, true and false, null, lists, and objects, so Jackson can fill a record's fields with real values: `{"attendees": 3}` arrives as the number 3. But JSON has no type for dates, so a time like `"2026-10-05T14:00:00Z"` arrives as a string, and Jackson turns it into a Java time only because the record asks for one. And the client chose every value, so a field you expect might be missing, or the wrong type. The lesson on validation and errors checks every value at the edge, and this lesson shows where each one comes from.

The example below makes all of this visible, with a small controller that answers with exactly what it received.

examples.title: A controller that echoes what it got
examples.prompt: A demo, not part of Roombook: `src/main/java/dev/hackuniversity/roombook/demo/EchoController.java`. It sends back the parts of each POST it receives.
examples.explanation: Each parameter takes one part of the request, with no conversion: the path parameter as a `String`, the whole query string as a `MultiValueMap`, a map whose every key can hold several values, one header, and the body as a `JsonNode`, Jackson's general type for any JSON, from `tools.jackson.databind`. The handler packs them into a small record, and Jackson writes it back out as JSON. The header is asked for as `content-type` in lowercase on purpose, as the next example shows.

examples.title: Sending it every kind of data
examples.prompt: One request with a path parameter, two query parameters, one of them twice, and a JSON body. The quotes around the URL stop the terminal from reading `&` as its own symbol.
examples.explanation: `roomId` is `"3"`, a string, though it looks like a number. The query came back as lists of strings: `date` has one value and `amenity` has both, which the next part relies on. `content-type` was found even though curl sent `Content-Type`, since header names ignore capital letters. In the body, `attendees` is the number 3 and `note` is a real `null`, because JSON has those types. Every value from outside the body came in as text.

steps.title: Query parameters: filters, sorting, and pages

examples.title: Filtering by building and amenity
examples.prompt: Rooms in the Main Library that have a whiteboard. The URL is in quotes because of the `&`.
examples.explanation: Hopper is in the Science Library, so the building filter dropped it. Lovelace and Turing both have a whiteboard. They come back sorted by name, the default, so Lovelace is first. Both fit on one page of 20, so `nextCursor` is `null`: there's nothing more to fetch. A client checks that one field to know whether to ask again, instead of guessing from how many items came back.

examples.title: Two pages, two rooms at a time
examples.prompt: The first command sorts by capacity with pages of 2, and `-w '\n'` ends its answer with a line break. The second sends back the `nextCursor` the first one returned.
examples.explanation: The first page holds the two smallest rooms, Lovelace with 4 and Turing with 6, and a cursor. Decoded, `Niwx` is just `6,1`: after the room with capacity 6 and id 1, which is Turing. The second page starts right after it, with Hopper, and its `nextCursor` is `null`, since that was the last room. The client never had to know what was inside the cursor, only to pass it back.

examples.title: Two kinds of bad value
examples.prompt: The first asks for 500 rooms in one page, with `-w '\n'` to end its answer with a line break. The second sends text where a number belongs.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 422
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 67
Date: Sun, 22 Nov 2026 00:00:32 GMT

{"status":422,"title":"limit must be a whole number from 1 to 100"}
HTTP/1.1 400
Content-Type: application/json
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Date: Sun, 22 Nov 2026 00:00:32 GMT
Connection: close

{"timestamp":"2026-11-22T00:00:32.099Z","status":400,"error":"Bad Request","message":"Method parameter 'minCapacity': Failed to convert value of type 'java.lang.String' to required type 'java.lang.Integer'; For input string: \"lots\"","path":"/v1/rooms"}
examples.explanation: 500 is a fine number that breaks Roombook's rule, so `RoomQuery.of` threw, and the controller answered 422 with the rule as the title. `lots` never reached Roombook's code: Spring couldn't make an `Integer` of it and answered 400 in Spring Boot's own format, and closed the connection. By Roombook's contract, both are readable requests with a bad value, so both should be 422, and the lesson on validation and errors makes Spring's conversion errors answer that way. Quietly using 100 instead of 500 would have hidden the client's mistake: they'd think they got everything.

steps.title: Headers: about the request and the answer
steps.body:
Headers are where a request and a response describe themselves: what format they're in, who's asking, and under what conditions. They're easy to overlook, since curl hides them unless you ask, and they're behind some of an API's most useful tricks, like answering a repeated read with no body at all.

## Request headers Roombook reads

| Header | What it says | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `Content-Type` | the format of the body | `application/json` |
| `Accept` | the formats the client can read | `application/json` |
| `Authorization` | the caller's credentials | `Bearer eyJhbGciOi...` |
| `If-None-Match` | send it only if it changed | `"0f34015334b3e0..."` |
| `If-Match` | change it only if it hasn't changed | `"3"` |
| `Idempotency-Key` | a retry of an earlier request | `9f1c2e7a-...` |

The lesson on logins reads `Authorization`, the lesson on data integrity uses `If-Match`, and the reliability lesson uses `Idempotency-Key`. In Spring, a handler asks for one by name, and `required = false` makes it `null` when it's missing:

```java
@RequestHeader(name = "Idempotency-Key", required = false) String idempotencyKey
```

## Response headers Roombook sends

| Header | What it says |
|---|---|
| `Location` | where the new or moved resource is |
| `Cache-Control` | who may keep a copy of the answer, and for how long |
| `ETag` | a fingerprint of this version of the resource |
| `Retry-After` | how long to wait before trying again, after a 429 or 503 |

`Cache-Control` suits data that rarely changes. Roombook's buildings change about once a year, so `buildings/BuildingController.java` says any cache may keep the list for five minutes:

```java
@GetMapping
public ResponseEntity<Page<Building>> list() {
    return ResponseEntity.ok()
            .cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(Duration.ofMinutes(5)).cachePublic())
            .body(new Page<>(BUILDINGS, null));
}
```

`public` means any cache along the way may store it, and `max-age=300` means for 300 seconds. Answers that depend on who's asking, like a user's own bookings, must never be `public`, or a shared cache could hand one person's bookings to another. For those, use `CacheControl.noStore()` or `cachePrivate()`, which the Redis lesson comes back to.

## Two rules for names

Header names ignore capital letters: `Content-Type`, `content-type`, and `CONTENT-TYPE` are the same header, and Spring finds any spelling. HTTP/2, recall from the web course, even sends them all in lowercase.

A header you invent needs no `X-` at the start. That prefix was once the custom for headers outside the standards, but headers that started as `X-` and later became standard had to keep the awkward name forever, so the custom was dropped in 2012. That's why it's `Idempotency-Key`, not `X-Idempotency-Key`. You'll still meet old ones like `X-Request-Id`, which the middleware lesson uses because everyone already does.

## ETag and 304: nothing new to send

An `ETag` is a fingerprint of a response's body. A client that saved the room, and its `ETag`, can later ask for it again with `If-None-Match` and the fingerprint. If the room is unchanged, the fingerprint matches, and the server answers **304 Not Modified** with no body: your copy is still good. If it changed, the client gets a normal 200 with the new room and a new `ETag`.

Spring doesn't add ETags until you ask. Roombook asks with one bean in `config/WebConfig.java`. A method marked `@Bean` hands Spring an object to keep as a bean, which the lesson on layers explains in full:

```java
@Bean
public ShallowEtagHeaderFilter etagFilter() {
    return new ShallowEtagHeaderFilter();
}
```

A **filter** is code that runs around every request before Spring MVC sees it, which the middleware lesson covers. This one holds back each response's body, computes an MD5 hash of it, a short fingerprint of the bytes, and either sends it as the `ETag` or, when it matches `If-None-Match`, swaps the response for a 304. Since it holds the whole body anyway, it also sets `Content-Length`.

That saves the bandwidth of the body, which matters on a phone, and browsers do it on their own for anything they've cached. It doesn't save the server's work, since the handler built the whole answer to fingerprint it, which is what shallow means here. The lesson on data integrity gives each room a version number, which makes an ETag Roombook can check without building the body, and lets `If-Match` stop two people's edits from overwriting each other.

examples.title: Asking again with If-None-Match
examples.prompt: The first command reads room 1 and shows its `ETag`, with `-w '\n'` to end the answer with a line break. The second sends that `ETag` back.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200
ETag: "0f34015334b3e0ed0091e236374a35cb8"
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 99
Date: Sun, 22 Nov 2026 00:00:32 GMT

{"id":1,"name":"Turing","building":"main-library","capacity":6,"amenities":["whiteboard","screen"]}
HTTP/1.1 304
ETag: "0f34015334b3e0ed0091e236374a35cb8"
Date: Sun, 22 Nov 2026 00:00:32 GMT
examples.explanation: The first answer is a full 200 with the room, 99 bytes, and its fingerprint. The second is a 304 with the same `ETag` and no body, since the room hadn't changed. The filter compared the fingerprints after the handler ran, and threw the body away. The `0` at the start of the value is the filter's own marker, and the rest is the hash. Change the room with a PATCH, and the same second command gets a 200 again, with the new room and a new fingerprint.

examples.title: The buildings list, with Cache-Control
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200
Cache-Control: max-age=300, public
ETag: "0d0318c10088d25d4e6dd9756c0385af3"
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 275
Date: Sun, 22 Nov 2026 00:00:32 GMT

{"items":[{"id":1,"slug":"main-library","name":"Main Library","timezone":"America/New_York","opensAt":"08:00","closesAt":"22:00"},{"id":2,"slug":"science-library","name":"Science Library","timezone":"America/New_York","opensAt":"09:00","closesAt":"18:00"}],"nextCursor":null}
examples.explanation: Spring wrote the directives as `max-age=300, public`, the same rule in another order. A browser that calls this from a web page keeps the answer for five minutes, and repeats within that time never reach Roombook at all. After that, it asks again with `If-None-Match`, and gets a 304 while the list is unchanged. Each building has its slug, the name the rooms filter uses, and its opening hours, written as local times in the building's time zone, `America/New_York`, which later lessons need to check that a booking falls inside them.

steps.title: The request body

examples.title: A form post instead of JSON
examples.prompt: `-d` on its own sends the body as form data, the way an HTML form would.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 415
Accept: application/json, application/*+json
Content-Type: application/json
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Date: Sun, 22 Nov 2026 00:00:32 GMT

{"timestamp":"2026-11-22T00:00:32.141Z","status":415,"error":"Unsupported Media Type","message":"Content-Type 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded;charset=UTF-8' is not supported.","path":"/v1/rooms"}
examples.explanation: curl sent `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, and the `create` handler's `@RequestBody RoomInput` has no converter for that type, so Spring refused it before the handler ran. The `message` names the type it got, and the `Accept` header names the ones it reads, which tells the client's developer exactly what to fix: send JSON. The handler never saw a half-read body, so nothing was created.

examples.title: Too big, and broken
examples.prompt: `big.json` is a 200 KB booking with a very long note, saved in the folder you run curl from. The second body is JSON cut off halfway. `-w '%{http_code}'` prints only the status code.
examples.explanation: The `@` in `--json @big.json` tells curl to send the file's contents. The interceptor saw a `Content-Length` over 100 KB and answered 413 with `{"status":413,"title":"Request body too large"}`, and nothing read the body. The broken body got a 400 from Spring, since it couldn't be parsed at all. That's the 400 and 422 split from the routes lesson: 400 when the request can't be read, 422 when it can, and a value breaks a rule.

examples.title: Keeping a note, then clearing it
examples.prompt: Booking 1002 has the note Chemistry revision, from the first example in the next part. The first patch leaves the note out, and the second sets it to null. `-w '\n'` keeps the two answers on separate lines.
examples.code:
curl -w '\n' -X PATCH --json '{"attendees": 4}' http://localhost:8080/v1/bookings/1002
curl -X PATCH --json '{"note": null}' http://localhost:8080/v1/bookings/1002
examples.explanation: After the first patch, `attendees` is 4 and the note is untouched, since `has("note")` was false. After the second, the note is `null`, since the field was there with `null` as its value. `version` went up with each change, as the repository's `update` does every time. If your server restarted, booking 1002 is gone, so run the next part's first example before these two.

steps.title: Responses and the handler's job
steps.body:
A handler's last step, the response, is the contract clients code against. Every field name, every time format, and every null is something a web app or a phone app will depend on, and changing it later breaks them. So Roombook decides these once, and every handler follows the same rules.

## Parse, check, act, respond

Every handler does the same four things, in this order:

1. **Parse**: turn the request's text into values, like an id from the path or a `RoomQuery` from the query string.
2. **Check**: refuse what's wrong, with the right code, before changing anything. Is the id valid, is the room there, are the values allowed.
3. **Act**: do the work, usually through the repository.
4. **Respond**: turn the result into JSON, with the right status and headers.

Keeping that order means a request that fails a check never changes anything, so an error never leaves half a booking behind. In Spring, a lot of the parsing happens before your method runs, in the annotated parameters. The lesson on validation and errors moves the checks into annotations on the records, and the lesson on layers moves the act step into a service, but the order stays.

## Roombook's JSON rules

- **Field names are camelCase**, like `startsAt` and `roomId`: the style of Java's own field names, and of most JSON APIs. Jackson uses a record's component names as they are.
- **Times are strings in RFC 3339 format, in UTC, to the second**, like `"2026-10-05T14:00:00Z"`. RFC 3339 is the standard way to write a date and time, and the `Z` at the end means UTC, the time zone with no offset. One zone for every time means a client never has to guess. Roombook keeps times as `java.time.Instant`, a moment on the UTC timeline, and Jackson writes an `Instant` exactly this way.
- **Ids are whole numbers**, like `1002`, a `long` in Java.
- **Every field is always there.** A note that's empty is `"note": null`, never a missing field. Jackson writes `null` fields by default, so a client can rely on the shape without checking first whether a field exists.
- **Lists are objects**: `{"items": [...], "nextCursor": ...}`, even when there's only one page. A small generic record holds that shape: `record Page<T>(List<T> items, String nextCursor)`.

## Never send what you store

From this lesson on, Roombook's bookings repository stores times as `Instant`s, the way the raw SQL lesson's database code will hand them back. The stored record also has fields that aren't part of the contract, like `cancelledAt`, the moment a booking was cancelled, which Roombook keeps for its own records. So no handler returns a stored `Booking` as it is. Each one returns a **view**, a record that holds exactly the JSON the contract promises, in `bookings/BookingView.java`:

```java
public record BookingView(
        long id,
        long roomId,
        long userId,
        Instant startsAt,
        Instant endsAt,
        int attendees,
        String note,
        BookingStatus status,
        int version,
        Instant createdAt) {

    public static BookingView from(Booking booking) {
        return new BookingView(booking.id(), booking.roomId(), booking.userId(), booking.startsAt(),
                booking.endsAt(), booking.attendees(), booking.note(), booking.status(), booking.version(),
                booking.createdAt());
    }
}
```

Every handler that answers with a booking returns `BookingView.from(booking)`. It names each field, so `cancelledAt` stays inside, and a new field added to storage later, like a user's password hash in the lesson on logins, can never leak into a response by accident. It also lets storage change without changing the API, which is what the lesson on raw SQL will need when the records come from a database. Java's records make views cheap to write, and Jackson writes their fields in the order they're declared.

## Accept and 406

A client says which formats it can read in the `Accept` header. Roombook only speaks JSON, so a client that accepts only, say, `text/csv` can't be served, and the honest answer is **406 Not Acceptable**. Spring sends it by itself: ask for room 1 with `Accept: text/csv`, and the answer is a 406 with an empty body, since every format Spring could write the error in is one the client said it can't read. Most clients send `Accept: application/json` or `*/*`, which means anything.

examples.title: A booking made in another time zone
examples.prompt: A student's phone set to UTC+2 sends local times, written with a `+02:00` offset.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 201
Location: /v1/bookings/1002
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 209
Date: Sun, 22 Nov 2026 00:00:32 GMT

{"id":1002,"roomId":2,"userId":1,"startsAt":"2026-10-05T14:00:00Z","endsAt":"2026-10-05T15:00:00Z","attendees":2,"note":"Chemistry revision","status":"confirmed","version":1,"createdAt":"2026-10-01T09:00:00Z"}
examples.explanation: `CreateBookingRequest`, the record the body becomes, declares `startsAt` and `endsAt` as `Instant`, so Jackson parsed each time with its offset and stored the moment itself, and the view wrote it back in UTC: 16:00 at UTC+2 is 14:00 UTC. The client sent one format, and every client reads the same format back. `createdAt` comes from Roombook's story clock, 1 October 2026 at 9:00 UTC, which stands in for the real time. The lesson on layers shows where that clock lives, and the testing lesson how tests control it. The stored booking also has `cancelledAt`, set to `null`, and the view left it out.

examples.title: Reading a booking through its view
examples.prompt: The seeded booking, Ada's study group in Turing.
examples.explanation: Every field the contract promises is there, in the order the view declares them, in camelCase, with every time in UTC to the second. Monday 5 October from 14:00 to 15:30 UTC is a 90-minute booking, on the 30-minute boundaries Roombook's rules require. The same view serves the GET, the POST, the PATCH, and the cancel action, so all four answers have the same shape, and a client needs only one type for a booking. The next lesson adds the code that runs around every one of these handlers: middleware.

recap:
- The path names the thing, the query string holds options, headers describe the request, the body carries content, and cookies carry the session.
- Path, query, and headers arrive as text, Spring converts them for typed parameters, and text that won't convert gets a 400.
- `@RequestParam` takes defaults, `required = false`, and `List<String>` for repeated names, and RoomQuery refuses unknown names.
- Give list parameters defaults and bounds, sort from an allowlist, refuse unknown names, and page with an opaque cursor.
- Header names ignore case, new ones need no X- prefix, and ShallowEtagHeaderFilter gives ETags and 304s.
- Spring answers 415 and 400 for bodies by itself, and Roombook's interceptor adds the 413 limit that Spring lacks.
- A record can't tell a missing field from a null one, so a PATCH reads a JsonNode and asks has().
- Send camelCase JSON with Instant times in UTC and every field present, built by a view record, never the stored one.
